arXiv:2602.15332v1 [cs.LG] 17 Feb 2026

Directional Reasoning Trajectory Change (DRTC): Identifying Critical Trace Segments in Reasoning Models

Waldemar Chang Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University Email: wchang58@jh.edu
Abstract

Understanding how language models carry out long-horizon reasoning remains an open challenge. Existing interpretability methods often highlight tokens or spans correlated with an answer, but they rarely reveal where the model makes consequential reasoning turns, which earlier context causally triggers those turns, or whether the highlighted text actually steers the reasoning process. We introduce Directional Reasoning Trajectory Change (DRTC), a process-causal framework for interpreting long-form reasoning from a single on-policy rollout. DRTC first detects pivot decision points using uncertainty and distribution-shift signals, then applies receiver-side interventions that preserve the realized rollout without resampling the continuation while blocking information flow from selected earlier chunks only at a pivot. It quantifies whether each intervention redirects the direction of the model’s log-probability trajectory relative to the realized rollout direction, producing a signed per-chunk attribution score. We additionally compute turning-angle curvature changes on raw logits as a complementary diagnostic and introduce curvature signatures to summarize shared intervention-response geometry via curvature role paths. Empirically, DRTC acts like a “steering map” for long traces, yielding a compact ranked shortlist of influential chunks: across four reasoning models spanning multiple backbone families, directional influence is sharply concentrated (per-example |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| shares yield Gini ≈0.50\approx 0.50–0.580.58 and top-5%5\% mass ≈0.23\approx 0.23–0.280.28), and learned pivots induce stronger intervention magnitudes than matched random spans. In a scaling study on 500 MATH problems with R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, learned spans continue to outperform matched random spans (median Δ=0.409\Delta=0.409, 355/500 positive; sign test p=2.3×10−21p=2.3\times 10^{-21}). Overall, DRTC provides a causally grounded, trajectory-level view of how specific context elements steer reasoning under on-policy dynamics.

1 Introduction

Reasoning models increasingly solve problems by generating long, winding traces with backtracking, verification, and strategy shifts, rather than simple forward inference (Kim et al., 2026). This creates a central interpretability gap: for many deployments, we do not just want to know what a model answered, but how it got there—when it changed its mind, what information triggered the change, and which earlier context causally shaped the computation that followed.

Why standard interpretability breaks for reasoning traces.

Consider a common pattern in math and planning: the model writes dozens of sentences pursuing an incorrect approach, then produces a “wait”-style hesitation, checks its work, abandons the approach, adopts a new strategy, and only much later commits to the final answer (Lee and Hockenmaier, 2025; Huang et al., 2025). In such traces, it is not clear which internal computation should be analyzed, since modern reasoning chains interleave exploratory, corrective, and outcome-determining steps, and a single sampled trace need not cleanly reflect the underlying causal structure (Macar et al., 2025). Studying the forward pass that emits the final answer is often unhelpful: long-horizon generation is mediated by intermediate reasoning steps, later tokens depend on earlier commitments, and multi-token answers introduce additional sequential dependencies (Pan et al., 2026; Ling et al., 2023). More fundamentally, the reasoning process is path-dependent: once the model commits to a line of thought, subsequent generations are constrained by that commitment, making it ill-posed to isolate a single decisive computation. Causal interventions are likewise difficult to interpret: editing the trace while holding later text fixed is off-policy, whereas resampling after an edit often produces a qualitatively different trajectory that is hard to compare (Macar et al., 2025). These issues reflect a deeper fact: long-horizon reasoning is a sampled, sequential computation with serial depth that exceeds a single forward pass, and standard attribution tools are poorly matched to this regime (Emmons et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026).

What we need instead.

These failure modes suggest that analyzing a single forward pass or performing unrestricted trace edits is insufficient. Instability is also not incidental: when the next-token distribution is flat (high entropy / low margin), multiple continuations are plausible, and prior work shows it is beneficial to focus exploration or intervention on these high-uncertainty steps, whereas low-uncertainty steps can be followed greedily (Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). An adequate method must therefore (i) localize such critical decision moments within a realized trace, and (ii) perform temporally valid causal tests of whether specific earlier context segments influenced the model at those moments, while preserving the realized rollout as the reference trajectory rather than editing the trace or resampling alternative continuations. This should remain meaningful even when “the outcome” is ambiguous (open-ended tasks) or not yet produced (truncated rollouts), since many real settings involve unfinished or non-terminal reasoning.

Our approach: Directional Reasoning Trajectory Change (DRTC).

We introduce Directional Reasoning Trajectory Change (DRTC), a process-causal framework for interpreting long-horizon reasoning from a single on-policy rollout. DRTC makes four methodological contributions:

  • •

    Pivot-localized decision-point discovery: We identify decision pivots within a realized chain-of-thought using uncertainty and distribution-shift signals (entropy, top-2 margin, and Jensen–Shannon divergence), targeting moments where the computation is unstable and strategy may change.

  • •

    Temporally valid, on-policy causal interventions: At each pivot, we apply receiver-side attention masking that preserves the realized rollout without resampling the continuation while blocking information flow from selected earlier chunks only at that pivot, yielding deterministic chunk–pivot causal effects and enabling screening gates that downweight noisy probes.

  • •

    Directional trajectory attribution as the causal target: We measure whether each intervention redirects the direction of the model’s log-probability trajectory relative to the realized rollout direction, aggregating pivot importance, causal relevance, and directional effect into a signed per-chunk attribution score rather than relying on final-answer flips or likelihood-only criteria.

  • •

    Curvature-signature diagnostics from intervention-response geometry: We compute turning-angle curvature changes in logit space as a complementary diagnostic signal and introduce curvature signatures that summarize how masking a chunk changes turning angles across pivots; cosine similarity between signatures defines curvature similarity between chunks. These signatures induce diagnostic curvature roles that group chunks by shared intervention-response geometry; in qualitative inspection, roles often align with semantically coherent trace segments, enabling compact pivot-aligned role paths.

Diagnostics and artifacts for verification.

To enable reviewer-auditable inspection, each run exports full provenance artifacts grounded in the model’s exact tokenized input. These include: (i) per-example summary tables with pivot statistics and attribution aggregates, (ii) per-configuration ranked chunk lists with stable chunk identifiers, (iii) integrity-checked mappings between chunk indices and token spans, and (iv) a self-contained interactive HTML reviewer interface that links raw text, pivot locations, masking interventions, and trajectory visualization (Figure ).

All reported DRTC and curvature quantities are reproducible directly from the exported JSON bundles without re-running model inference. This design allows reviewers to verify pivot discovery, intervention construction, per-pivot effects (δk,i,wk,i)(\delta_{k,i},w_{k,i}), and final aggregation mechanics step-by-step on the exact realized rollout.

In practice, the signed per-chunk scores are sharply concentrated, yielding a compact, auditable shortlist of context segments to inspect within long traces and a concrete, mechanically grounded starting point for subsequent circuit-level or mechanistic analyses.

2 Related work

Recent interpretability work has shifted from single-pass explanations toward causal analysis of multi-step reasoning traces. Zhao et al. (2026) formalize decorative thinking, showing that only a small fraction of chain-of-thought steps exert meaningful causal influence; their True Thinking Score (TTS) estimates causal contribution via stochastic perturbation and resampling. Macar et al. (2025) similarly argue that a single realized trace is insufficient and use on-policy resampling to study the resilience of semantic content across trajectories. Complementary work models causal influence across autoregressive generations: Walker and Ewetz (2025) construct attribution graphs that quantify dependence on the prompt and prior outputs while preserving causal structure. In parallel, geometric approaches treat reasoning as a trajectory in representation space: Zhou et al. (2025) relate logical structure to trajectory geometry and analyze discrete turning behavior, while Curved Inference measures residual-stream bending under a pullback semantic metric derived from the unembedding map (Manson, 2025). Other studies analyze logit and layer-wise dynamics for interpretability and decoding, including DeLTa’s logit-trajectory prediction strategy for decoding (He et al., 2025) and stage-wise analyses of arithmetic signal progression across layers (Yan, 2025).

DRTC targets a distinct explanatory object: which earlier context chunks causally steer a realized long-horizon reasoning trace under on-policy generation. It uses pivot-local, deterministic receiver-side interventions and a directional trajectory target in log-probability space, with curvature used only as a complementary diagnostic of intervention-induced reorientation. A detailed comparison to resampling-based methods, attribution graphs, geometry-first analyses, and layer-wise dynamics appears in Appendix C (Table 17).

3 Methodology

3.1 Overview

DRTC attributes long-horizon reasoning by combining (i) pivot discovery to localize consequential decision points in a single on-policy rollout, (ii) receiver-side interventions that block information from specific earlier chunks only at those pivots while preserving the realized generated text, and (iii) a directional causal target that measures whether an intervention redirects the model’s log-probability trajectory toward or away from the realized rollout direction. We also compute turning-angle curvature in logit space as a complementary geometric diagnostic. Curvature is never used to select pivots or define DRTC scores.

3.2 Problem setup

Given a prompt, the model produces a single on-policy autoregressive reasoning rollout with tokens {yt}t=1T\{y_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. We segment the rollout text into NN contiguous fixed-stride chunks {c1,…,cN}\{c_{1},\dots,c_{N}\} for attribution; prompt text and ground-truth solutions are retained for auditability but excluded from pivot discovery, interventions, and scoring. We use fixed-stride token chunks (16 tokens) rather than sentence segmentation to keep interventions length-controlled and reproducible under tokenization, avoid confounding ablation effect size with variable-length units, and keep long-horizon attribution tractable (Kiss and Strunk, 2006; Fong et al., 2019; DeYoung et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2026).

At step tt, the model defines a distribution pt​(⋅)p_{t}(\cdot) over the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} with logits zt∈ℝ|𝒱|z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}. We perform directional comparisons in log-probability space,

st=log⁡pt​(⋅)=log⁡softmax⁡(zt)∈ℝ|𝒱|,s_{t}\;=\;\log p_{t}(\cdot)\;=\;\log\softmax(z_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}, (1)

and compute curvature diagnostics separately in raw logit space. Our objective is to identify which chunks causally influence key decision points and whether that influence steers the reasoning trajectory along the realized rollout.

3.3 Pivot discovery and weighting

DRTC identifies a small set of pivot positions where the model is likely to commit, revise, or redirect its reasoning. For each position tt we compute an uncertainty/shift-based pivot score

u~t=γH​Ht+γM​(1−margint)+γS​St,\tilde{u}_{t}=\gamma_{H}H_{t}+\gamma_{M}\bigl(1-\mathrm{margin}_{t}\bigr)+\gamma_{S}S_{t}, (2)

where HtH_{t} is entropy, margint\mathrm{margin}_{t} is the top-2 probability margin, and StS_{t} is a local distribution-shift signal measured by Jensen–Shannon divergence between token windows before and after tt. We use (γH,γM,γS)=(1.0,1.0,0.5)(\gamma_{H},\gamma_{M},\gamma_{S})=(1.0,1.0,0.5).

We select the top KK pivots {τk}k=1K\{\tau_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} by u~t\tilde{u}_{t} subject to spacing constraints and assign each pivot a normalized importance weight via a softmax:

uk=exp⁡(u~τk)∑j=1Kexp⁡(u~τj),∑k=1Kuk=1.u_{k}\;=\;\frac{\exp(\tilde{u}_{\tau_{k}})}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\tilde{u}_{\tau_{j}})},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}=1. (3)

Uniform pivot weights are used as an ablation.

3.4 Receiver-side interventions and relevance screening

At each pivot τk\tau_{k}, we test whether an earlier chunk cic_{i} is causally relevant by applying a receiver-side intervention that blocks information flow from cic_{i} only at τk\tau_{k}. Concretely, we implement this as attention-edge masking at the prediction position, leaving the realized prefix unchanged while testing which earlier positions can influence the pivot distribution; similar edge-level and activation-patching interventions are standard tools in mechanistic interpretability (Geva et al., 2023; Conmy et al., 2023; Zhang and Nanda, 2024).

Let ℓt​(⋅)\ell_{t}(\cdot) denote pre-softmax logits. We define a pivot-local screening effect on the baseline top token yτk⋆y_{\tau_{k}}^{\star}:

ak,i=ℓτk​(yτk⋆)−ℓτk(−i,k)​(yτk⋆),a_{k,i}=\ell_{\tau_{k}}(y_{\tau_{k}}^{\star})-\ell_{\tau_{k}}^{(-i,k)}(y_{\tau_{k}}^{\star}), (4)

where (−i,k)(-i,k) denotes masking chunk cic_{i} at pivot τk\tau_{k}. Intuitively, ak,ia_{k,i} measures whether removing cic_{i} weakens the pivot decision.

We map screening effects to a bounded relevance gate

wk,i=σ⁡(βk​a^k,i)∈[0,1],w_{k,i}\;=\;\sigma\!\left(\beta_{k}\,\hat{a}_{k,i}\right)\in[0,1], (5)

where a^k,i\hat{a}_{k,i} is a robustly scaled version of ak,ia_{k,i} and βk\beta_{k} is a pivot-specific calibration parameter (chosen from the median magnitude of nonzero effects). The gate downweights chunk–pivot pairs that do not reliably affect the pivot decision while preserving ordering among stronger effects.

3.5 Directional trajectory change and DRTC aggregation

We model reasoning as a trajectory through log-probability space and measure whether an intervention redirects that trajectory along the realized rollout direction. Let sts_{t} and st(−i,k)s_{t}^{(-i,k)} denote the baseline and intervened log-probability vectors. We define a global rollout direction using the endpoints of the pivot sequence:

g=sτK−sτ1‖sτK−sτ1‖.g\;=\;\frac{s_{\tau_{K}}-s_{\tau_{1}}}{\|s_{\tau_{K}}-s_{\tau_{1}}\|}. (6)

For each pivot τk\tau_{k} and chunk cic_{i}, define the pivot-local trajectory effect

ek,i=sτk−sτk(−i,k),e_{k,i}\;=\;s_{\tau_{k}}-s_{\tau_{k}}^{(-i,k)}, (7)

and its directional component

δk,i=⟨ek,i,g⟩.\delta_{k,i}\;=\;\langle e_{k,i},g\rangle. (8)

Positive δk,i\delta_{k,i} indicates that chunk cic_{i} supports the realized rollout direction at pivot kk. For stability, we robustly normalize δk,i\delta_{k,i} within each pivot (median/MAD scaling with clipping; details in Appendix).

Finally, we aggregate across pivots using pivot weights and relevance gates:

DRTC⁡(i)=∑k=1Kuk​wk,i​δk,i.\mathrm{DRTC}(i)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}\,w_{k,i}\,\delta_{k,i}. (9)

We treat DRTC⁡(i)\mathrm{DRTC}(i) as the primary attribution score; auxiliary diagnostic decompositions are used only for internal checks and are reported in the Appendix.

3.6 Curvature diagnostics, signatures, and similarity

In addition to directional alignment, we compute a geometric diagnostic of how interventions change local turning behavior. Curvature is computed in raw logit space. For consecutive logits (zt−1,zt,zt+1)(z_{t-1},z_{t},z_{t+1}), define

vprev=zt−zt−1,vnext=zt+1−zt,κ⁡(zt−1,zt,zt+1)=arccos⁡(⟨vprev,vnext⟩‖vprev‖​‖vnext‖),v_{\mathrm{prev}}=z_{t}-z_{t-1},\qquad v_{\mathrm{next}}=z_{t+1}-z_{t},\qquad\kappa(z_{t-1},z_{t},z_{t+1})=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\langle v_{\mathrm{prev}},v_{\mathrm{next}}\rangle}{\|v_{\mathrm{prev}}\|\,\|v_{\mathrm{next}}\|}\right), (10)

with standard clipping and small-ε\varepsilon stabilization in implementation. For each pivot τk\tau_{k} and chunk cic_{i}, we measure the curvature change induced by the intervention:

Δ​κk,i=κ⁡(zτk−1,zτk(−i,k),zτk+1)−κ⁡(zτk−1,zτk,zτk+1),CurvImpact⁡(i)=∑k=1Kuk​Δ​κk,i.\Delta\kappa_{k,i}=\kappa(z_{\tau_{k}-1},z_{\tau_{k}}^{(-i,k)},z_{\tau_{k}+1})-\kappa(z_{\tau_{k}-1},z_{\tau_{k}},z_{\tau_{k}+1}),\qquad\mathrm{CurvImpact}(i)\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}\,\Delta\kappa_{k,i}. (11)

CurvImpact is diagnostic only: it describes intervention-response geometry and is not used as a causal attribution score.

We summarize curvature response patterns with a curvature signature vector

si=normalize⁡([Δ​κ1,i,…,Δ​κK,i]),s_{i}\;=\;\mathrm{normalize}\!\left([\Delta\kappa_{1,i},\dots,\Delta\kappa_{K,i}]\right),

and define curvature similarity between chunks ii and jj as ⟨si,sj⟩\langle s_{i},s_{j}\rangle. These quantities are used to group chunks into structural roles.

3.7 Curvature role paths: structural reorientation summaries

To compactly summarize long rollouts, we introduce curvature role paths, a diagnostic synopsis of major structural reorientations. We construct a graph whose nodes are chunks and whose edges connect pairs with curvature similarity above a fixed threshold; connected components define roles. Roles are purely structural groupings defined by curvature signatures and do not depend on DRTC or screening.

For each pivot τk\tau_{k}, we score the curvature reorientation contributed by a role rr as

RoleImpact⁡(r,k)=uk​∑ci∈r|Δ​κk,i|,\mathrm{RoleImpact}(r,k)\;=\;u_{k}\sum_{c_{i}\in r}|\Delta\kappa_{k,i}|,

select the role with maximal RoleImpact⁡(r,k)\mathrm{RoleImpact}(r,k), and choose a representative chunk with maximal |Δ​κk,i||\Delta\kappa_{k,i}| within that role. Ordering these dominant roles by pivot index yields a pivot-aligned curvature role path.

To distinguish structurally prominent but causally irrelevant reorientations from those that support the realized direction, we optionally annotate each role with aggregated DRTC:

DRTC⁡(r)=∑ci∈rDRTC⁡(i).\mathrm{DRTC}(r)\;=\;\sum_{c_{i}\in r}\mathrm{DRTC}(i).

This overlay is descriptive and does not affect role construction or pivot assignment. Overall, curvature role paths provide a compact qualitative summary of intervention-induced reorientation types that complements chunk-level DRTC attribution rather than replacing it.

4 Results

Setup.

We evaluate DRTC on a fixed 24-example slice from the math-rollouts problems, using the dataset only for problem statements (Bogdan et al., 2025). For each example, the model generates an on-policy autoregressive reasoning rollout (greedy decoding with fixed seeds), segmented into fixed-stride chunks for attribution; prompt text and ground truth are retained for auditability but excluded from pivot discovery, interventions, scoring, and qualitative ranking. Unless otherwise stated, we use K=8K=8 pivots per example.

We report results for four open-weight reasoning models: LFM2.5-1.2B-Thinking, Ministral-3B-Reasoning, Phi-4-Mini-Reasoning, and R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (AI, 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), evaluated on the same 24 examples with identical decoding settings and seeds. We compare C0 (DRTC only), C8 (pivot curvature diagnostics), and C9 (matched random-span control with identical masking and scoring logic).

4.1 Attribution invariance under curvature diagnostics

C0 and C8 differ only in whether curvature diagnostics are computed and logged; curvature is never used in pivot discovery, intervention construction, gating, or DRTC aggregation. We test invariance by computing, for each example, the Spearman rank correlation between per-chunk DRTC scores from C0 and C8. Across all four models (24 examples each), ρ=1.000\rho=1.000 for every example (median 1.0001.000, 95% CI [1.000,1.000][1.000,1.000]), with identity scatter and zero score differences within floating-point tolerance. Figure 2 shows a representative identity scatter for R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B; full per-model plots and auxiliary checks appear in Appendix A.1.

4.2 DRTC attribution is concentrated and structured

Across all models and configurations, DRTC attribution is concentrated rather than diffuse: a minority of chunks accounts for a disproportionate share of total directional influence. Using per-example normalized |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| mass shares, median Gini coefficients range from 0.500.50–0.580.58, and the top 5%5\% of chunks account for roughly 0.230.23–0.280.28 of total influence. Cross-model histograms, concentration curves, and bootstrap confidence intervals are provided in Appendix A.2 (see Fig. 6).

4.3 Pivot weighting is non-redundant

We test whether pivot importance weighting (uku_{k}) meaningfully affects attribution by recomputing DRTC scores post hoc with uniform pivot weights. Specifically, using the same per-pivot quantities (δk,i,wk,i)(\delta_{k,i},w_{k,i}) obtained from C0/C8/C9, we recompute

DRTCuniform​(i)=∑k1K​wk,i​δk,i,\mathrm{DRTC}_{\text{uniform}}(i)=\sum_{k}\tfrac{1}{K}\,w_{k,i}\,\delta_{k,i},

replacing learned uku_{k} with 1/K1/K. Because uku_{k} enters only in the final aggregation and does not influence δk,i\delta_{k,i} or wk,iw_{k,i}, this procedure is mathematically equivalent to rerunning the method with uniform pivot weights.

Across all models, Spearman correlations between weighted and uniform rankings remain high (ρ≈0.97\rho\approx 0.97–0.990.99), but strictly less than 1. Equivalent ablations for all four models, including weighted-vs-uniform scatter plots and per-model summary statistics, are provided in Appendix A.6.

Correlations are high but strictly below 1.000, indicating that pivot importance weighting preserves the dominant attribution structure while introducing non-trivial reshuffling of chunk rankings. This contrasts with the C0 vs. C8 comparison (Section 4.1), where correlations are identically 1.000, confirming that curvature logging is purely diagnostic whereas pivot weighting modulates attribution aggregation.

4.4 Random-span falsification: intervention magnitude

We evaluate whether learned pivots (C8) produce meaningfully stronger interventions than matched random spans (C9). As the primary falsification signal, we compute the per-example mean absolute pivot-local intervention magnitude, 𝔼k​[|δk,i|]\mathbb{E}_{k}[|\delta_{k,i}|]. Across all four models, C8 exhibits strictly higher median per-example intervention magnitude than C9, with median gaps (C8 −- C9) ranging from +0.039+0.039 to +0.178+0.178 and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown in Figure 3. C8 exceeds C9 for the majority of examples (see Appendix A.3). This effect is consistent across examples rather than driven by a small number of outliers. Additional rank-stability diagnostics (e.g., δ\delta-vs-full Spearman) appear in Appendix A.3.

4.5 Curvature provides a complementary geometric diagnostic

Within C8, curvature is a complementary geometric diagnostic: across models, |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}| is positively associated with |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}|, while signed CurvImpact\mathrm{CurvImpact} has near-zero association with signed DRTC\mathrm{DRTC}. This is consistent with curvature tracking reorientation intensity rather than directional steering, and it is not used in pivots, gating, or attribution. Aggregate statistics and visual diagnostics are in Appendix A.4.

4.6 Adjacency and shuffle controls

We test whether attribution and curvature structure are trivial consequences of proximity. Adjacent chunks (|Δ​i|≤1|\Delta i|\leq 1 from the pivot-containing chunk) have higher mean |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| than distant chunks (|Δ​i|≥5|\Delta i|\geq 5), with ratios of roughly 22–3×3\times across models (Appendix A.5, Table 5). However, distant chunks retain non-zero mean influence, so DRTC is not fully explained by adjacency.

For curvature roles, we apply a shuffle control: randomly permuting curvature signatures collapses the real CurvImpact–DRTC association toward zero, while the unshuffled assignments remain consistently positive (Appendix A.5, Fig. 10). This supports the claim that curvature similarity reflects structured intervention-response geometry rather than a clustering artifact.

4.7 Scaling study on MATH (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B)

To test robustness beyond the 24-example cross-architecture slice, we run DRTC on N=500N=500 MATH problems (Hendrycks et al., 2021) with R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (greedy decoding, fixed seeds, K=8K=8; median trace length 2694 tokens, IQR [2131, 3068]). The primary falsification gap persists at scale: learned spans (C8) produce stronger pivot-local directional interventions than matched random spans (C9), with median Δ=𝔼k​[|δ|]C8−𝔼k​[|δ|]C9=0.409\Delta=\mathbb{E}_{k}[|\delta|]_{\textsc{C8}}-\mathbb{E}_{k}[|\delta|]_{\textsc{C9}}=0.409 (95% CI [0.354, 0.453]) and Δ>0\Delta>0 for 355/500 examples (sign test p=2.3×10−21p=2.3\times 10^{-21}). Attribution remains moderately concentrated (median Gini 0.586; median top-1 mass 0.089; median top-5% mass 0.209), and curvature remains complementary rather than directional (median Spearman ρ⁡(|CurvImpact|,|DRTC|)=0.080\rho(|\mathrm{CurvImpact}|,|\mathrm{DRTC}|)=0.080; median signed ρ=−0.039\rho=-0.039). Full scaling statistics and curvature diagnostic visualizations are provided in Appendix A.3 and Appendix A.4 (e.g., Fig. 9).

4.8 Qualitative interpretation

Across all four models, DRTC yields consistent qualitative structure in how directional influence is distributed along reasoning traces. Top-magnitude DRTC chunks typically correspond to strategy-setting constraints or key structural commitments (e.g., introducing an algebraic invariant, applying a functional-iteration identity, or enforcing a conjugacy condition). Masking these segments produces the largest pivot-local redirections, consistent with them anchoring the realized trajectory.

Opposing-sign chunks are not arbitrary: they often align with early orientation text, exploratory detours, or provisional reasoning that is later revised. Masking such segments can increase alignment with the realized direction gg, indicating interpretable directional tension rather than noise. In parallel, chunks with large |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}| frequently coincide with visible phase transitions in the trace (e.g., restatement →\rightarrow derivation, manipulation →\rightarrow verification). While signed curvature–DRTC correlations remain near zero, curvature magnitude tracks attribution magnitude and stratifies the intensity of local reorientation without serving as a causal score. Detailed per-model case studies appear in Appendix B.

4.9 Summary: DRTC as a process-level steering map

Taken together, the results support DRTC as a process-level steering map for a single realized rollout. The invariance test (Section 4.1) cleanly separates directional attribution from auxiliary geometry logging, while the random-span falsification (Section 4.4) shows that learned pivots identify interventions that are stronger than matched controls under identical masking logic. The concentration results (Section 4.2) imply that DRTC produces an auditable shortlist of influential context segments rather than a diffuse heatmap, and the pivot-weight ablation (Section 4.3; Appendix A.6) confirms that pivot importance modulates aggregation rather than acting as a cosmetic reweighting. Curvature diagnostics (Section 4.5) provide a complementary view of reorientation intensity without functioning as an attribution score, and adjacency/shuffle controls (Section 4.6) reduce the risk that the observed structure is a trivial proximity artifact. Finally, the scaling study (Section 4.7) shows that the falsification signal and concentration behavior persist beyond the small cross-architecture slice.

5 Conclusion, limitations, and future work

Limitations.

DRTC measures directional redirection at pivot points rather than outcome-level causal effects on correctness, so steering need not imply answer changes. Attribution currently uses fixed-stride chunks and a fixed pivot budget (K=8K=8), which stabilizes comparisons but may miss the appropriate granularity of reasoning; adaptive pivots and variable-resolution or hierarchical chunking are natural extensions. Curvature is used strictly as a logit-space geometric descriptor and does not identify the circuits implementing reorientation, motivating integration with mechanistic tracing. Finally, broader evaluation across domains and decoding strategies, together with joint analysis of trajectory steering and outcome sensitivity, is needed to clarify when local redirections accumulate into correctness changes.

Conclusion.

We introduced Directional Reasoning Trajectory Change (DRTC), a process-causal interpretability framework for long-horizon reasoning under on-policy autoregressive generation. DRTC localizes pivot decision points and applies receiver-side interventions that block information flow from selected earlier chunks only at those pivots, yielding signed per-chunk steering scores defined by directional changes in log-probability space. Across four reasoning models, attribution is consistently sparse and structured, learned pivots induce stronger intervention magnitudes than matched random spans, and curvature provides complementary geometric diagnostics without altering DRTC scores. Overall, DRTC provides a trajectory-level account of how specific context elements steer reasoning, while remaining agnostic to outcome-level causality and circuit identification.

Ethics Statement

This work does not introduce new model architectures or collect new datasets. We propose an analysis framework for interpreting existing autoregressive reasoning models via pivot-local, receiver-side input attribution. Consistent with the goals of explainable AI, the method is intended to increase transparency and support auditing of model behavior. As such, it does not introduce material ethical risks beyond those inherent to the deployment and use of the underlying pretrained models and their generated outputs. We evaluate only on publicly available problem statements and do not use personally identifiable information.

Reproducibility Statement

We describe the full methodology in the paper, including pivot discovery signals, intervention definition, scoring, and aggregation, along with model and decoding settings. Our experiments use fixed seeds and export complete per-example artifacts (pivot locations, chunk boundaries/identifiers, intervention effects, and attribution scores) to enable independent auditing. Upon acceptance, we will publicly release the full implementation and evaluation code, including scripts to reproduce all figures and tables, as well as the self-contained interactive reviewer UI used for qualitative inspection. For this submission, the relevant code and artifacts will be provided as supplementary material.

Appendix

Appendix A Additional quantitative evidence

A.1 C0 vs. C8 invariance diagnostics

C0 (baseline) and C8 (curvature-enabled) differ only in whether curvature diagnostics are computed and logged. Curvature is not used in pivot discovery, receiver-side masking, relevance gating, or DRTC aggregation. We therefore test directly whether enabling curvature logging changes any attribution results.

Per-example rank invariance.

For each model and each example (24 per model), we compute the Spearman rank correlation between per-chunk DRTC scores produced under C0 and C8. Across all four models, every example yields

ρ=1.000.\rho=1.000.

The median Spearman correlation is 1.0001.000 with 95% bootstrap confidence interval [1.000,1.000][1.000,1.000] for each model.

Score-level identity.

Beyond rank invariance, we verify score-level equality. For every example across all models, the maximum absolute difference between corresponding C0 and C8 DRTC scores is zero within floating-point tolerance. Thus, enabling curvature logging does not alter attribution magnitudes.

Visual confirmation.

Figure 4 shows representative per-model scatter plots of C0 versus C8 DRTC scores. All points lie exactly on the identity line. Corresponding per-example histograms of Spearman correlations are degenerate at ρ=1\rho=1 for every model.

Conclusion.

These results establish exact attribution invariance between C0 and C8. Curvature computation is strictly diagnostic and does not influence pivot selection, intervention construction, gating, aggregation, or final DRTC rankings.

A.2 DRTC concentration across models

Concentration metrics.

Across models, DRTC influence is moderately concentrated rather than diffuse: using per-example normalized |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| mass shares (computed within each example and summarized as the median across 24 examples), baseline (C0) Gini ranges from 0.500.50–0.580.58, with the top 5%5\% of chunks carrying roughly 0.230.23–0.280.28 of total |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| mass. These are not extreme-sparsity values (e.g., Gini ≫0.8\gg 0.8), but they are consistent across architectures and sufficient to reject “everything matters equally.” (C8 matches C0 exactly by construction and is therefore omitted from the tables below.)

Architecture note.

LFM2.5 occasionally exhibits higher top-1 mass outliers than the transformer backbones (Table 2). A plausible explanation is architectural inductive bias: LFM2.5 combines convolutional components with grouped-query attention, which may alter how influence concentrates across local versus long-range context [AI, 2025, Wu et al., 2019, Ainslie et al., 2023]. We leave targeted tests of this effect (e.g., locality vs. long-range dependence of top-attributed chunks) to future work.

A.3 Random-span falsification: magnitude primary, structure secondary

Primary metric (magnitude).

Pivot-associated spans (C8) produce stronger interventions than matched random spans (C9) across all four models. We quantify this using the per-example mean absolute pivot-local directional effect,

𝔼k​[|δk,i|],\mathbb{E}_{k}\bigl[|\delta_{k,i}|\bigr],

aggregated as the median across examples. We treat magnitude as the primary falsification signal because it directly measures effect strength rather than rank preservation.

Random-span falsification control (C8 vs. C9).

Both C8 and C9 use identical pivot discovery: we score token positions by uncertainty and distribution shift (entropy, top-2 margin, and local Jensen–Shannon divergence) and select the top-KK pivots under spacing constraints. The configurations differ only in which span of earlier tokens is treated as the candidate cause whose information flow is blocked at a pivot.

Pivot spans (C8). For each pivot, we define an associated span window [sk,ek)[s_{k},e_{k}) in the realized rollout (excluding prompt tokens), placed by the pivot/span selection procedure. Receiver-side masking then blocks attention from the pivot position τk\tau_{k} to tokens in this pivot-associated span.

Random spans (C9). After normal pivot discovery, we replace each pivot-associated span with a uniformly random span of identical length. Concretely, for a pivot span of length Lk=ek−skL_{k}=e_{k}-s_{k}, we sample a start index s~k\tilde{s}_{k} uniformly over rollout tokens (excluding prompt tokens), set e~k=s~k+Lk\tilde{e}_{k}=\tilde{s}_{k}+L_{k}, and reject samples that overlap protected regions (including the original pivot spans) up to a fixed retry budget. The causal intervention mechanism is otherwise unchanged: the model is probed by blocking attention from τk\tau_{k} to tokens in the (now random) control span.

What stays fixed vs. what changes. Pivot positions {τk}\{\tau_{k}\}, the masking operator, and span lengths {Lk}\{L_{k}\} are identical across C8 and C9; only span placement differs (pivot-associated vs. uniform random). Curvature logging, when enabled, remains strictly diagnostic in both conditions.

Interpretation. If DRTC is capturing meaningful causal influence, then masking pivot-associated spans (C8) should induce larger pivot-local trajectory effects than masking matched-length random spans (C9). We observe this consistently across models in the magnitude results reported in this section (see Fig. 3 in the main paper for the cross-model summary).

Metric clarification.

Table 3 reports stdd\mathrm{std}_{d}, our primary magnitude diagnostic (per-example mean absolute pivot-local intervention magnitude, summarized by the median across examples). In contrast, Figure 7 (top panel) reports the median per-example mean​|δk,i|\mathrm{mean}\,|\delta_{k,i}|, where δk,i=⟨ek,i,g⟩\delta_{k,i}=\langle e_{k,i},g\rangle is the signed directional projection used in DRTC aggregation. These quantities are related but not identical: stdd\mathrm{std}_{d} summarizes overall intervention magnitude at pivots, while mean​|δk,i|\mathrm{mean}\,|\delta_{k,i}| measures magnitude specifically along the realized rollout direction. Accordingly, absolute gap values differ across the table and figure, though both consistently show stronger effects for pivot-associated spans (C8) than matched random spans (C9).

Secondary metric (rank stability).

We also report δ\delta-vs-full Spearman as a rank-stability diagnostic. In Ministral-3-3B and Phi-4-Mini, C9 exceeds C8 on Spearman; we report this transparently and interpret it as a property of correlation-based rank preservation rather than stronger intervention magnitude.

A.4 Curvature diagnostic: geometry stratifies intervention-response types

Curvature (turning-angle / CurvImpact) is a diagnostic layer: it describes the geometry of intervention response rather than asserting causal influence on correctness. Absolute CurvImpact magnitudes vary substantially by architecture, but relative structure is stable within each model.

Representative curvature diagnostic visualization.

Figure 9 provides an intuition-building curvature diagnostic visualization comparing the pivot condition (C8) to the matched random-span control (C9). The left panel plots per-chunk DRTC⁡(i)\mathrm{DRTC}(i) against turning-angle curvature impact CurvImpact⁡(i)\mathrm{CurvImpact}(i) (computed in raw logit space) for a single example. Consistent with the aggregate results, signed CurvImpact\mathrm{CurvImpact} exhibits near-zero association with signed DRTC\mathrm{DRTC}, while larger reorientation intensity (higher |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}|) can coincide with larger directional attribution magnitude |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}|. The right panel provides a per-example summary of maximum |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}| under C8 and C9 as an auxiliary geometric diagnostic.

A.5 Adjacency effects and shuffle control

Adjacent chunks (near the pivot-containing chunk) have 2–3×\times higher mean |DRTC||\mathrm{DRTC}| contribution than distant chunks; this is expected because nearby text is more likely to be locally relevant. However, distant chunks retain non-trivial mean influence (Table 5), so DRTC is not fully explained by proximity. Moreover, proximity alone would predict that distance-matched random spans behave similarly to learned pivots; empirically, learned pivots induce larger intervention magnitudes than matched random spans (C8 vs. C9; Appendix A.3).

A.6 Pivot weighting (uku_{k}) concentration

Pivot weighting is concentrated: the maximum pivot weight per example is typically ≈0.15\approx 0.15–0.170.17, with similar entropy across models.

Appendix B Qualitative case studies

Reading guide.

Each case study reports: (i) problem and gold answer, (ii) top DRTC-contributing chunks (with excerpts), (iii) opposing-sign chunks, and (iv) large-magnitude curvature diagnostic chunks (CurvImpact). DRTC is process-causal: a chunk’s signed score indicates whether its pivot-local masking intervention pushes the pivot distribution toward (positive) or away from (negative) the realized rollout direction. CurvImpact is a diagnostic turning-angle signal computed in raw logit space and is not used to define pivots or compute DRTC. All interpretations are conservative: we do not make outcome-causal claims about correctness.

B.1 LFM2.5-1.2B

B.1.1 math_rollout_2312 (LFM2.5-1.2B)

Problem.

A nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients has all of the numbers 1+2,2+3,3+4,…,1000+10011+\sqrt{2},2+\sqrt{3},3+\sqrt{4},\dots,1000+\sqrt{1001} as roots.

Gold answer.

1970.

Opposing-sign chunks (directional tension).

Chunk 6 and chunk 52 have positive DRTC, meaning that (after pivot weighting and relevance gating) their information flow tends to redirect pivot log-probability vectors in the same direction as the realized rollout. Chunk 0 has negative DRTC, indicating that masking this early preamble makes the pivot-local change more aligned with the realized direction gg; this is consistent with generic orientation text contributing weak, possibly noisy steering relative to later problem-specific constraints.

Curvature diagnostic (geometry, not attribution).

CurvImpact is computed from changes in turning angles in raw logit space under the same pivot-local masking interventions. Large |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}| indicates interventions that materially change local trajectory geometry (reorientation intensity), but this signal is diagnostic and does not define causal importance or the sign of steering.

Qualitative interpretation.

Chunk 6 (the conjugate-root constraint) has the largest aggregated DRTC, i.e., the strongest pivot-weighted, gated directional effect among chunks in this rollout. This matches the core mathematical requirement for rational-coefficient polynomials: irrational roots must appear with their conjugates, except when n+1\sqrt{n+1} is integer (yielding a rational root). Given that the realized rollout is correct here, high positive DRTC chunks provide a compact shortlist of trace segments that most strongly support the realized solution path.

B.1.2 math_rollout_2757 (LFM2.5-1.2B)

Problem.

Let cc be a complex number. Suppose there exist distinct complex numbers rr, ss, and tt such that for every complex number zz, we have

(z−r)​(z−s)​(z−t)=(z−c​r)​(z−c​s)​(z−c​t).(z-r)(z-s)(z-t)=(z-cr)(z-cs)(z-ct).

Compute the number of distinct possible values of cc.

Gold answer.

44

Opposing-sign chunks (directional tension).

Chunks 4, 0, and 1 have positive DRTC, indicating that—after pivot weighting and relevance gating—their information flow tends to steer pivot-local distributions in the same direction as the realized rollout. Chunk 3 has negative DRTC, meaning that masking it makes the pivot-local trajectory more aligned with the realized direction gg. This suggests that portions of the raw polynomial equality restatement exert mild counter-steering relative to the algebraic constraint structure emphasized later in the trace.

Curvature diagnostic (geometry, not attribution).

CurvImpact measures how pivot-local masking alters turning angles in raw logit space. Chunk 4 and chunk 5 exhibit comparatively large |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}|, indicating substantial local geometric reorientation under intervention. As in other case studies, curvature reflects reorientation intensity rather than directional support, and does not determine causal sign.

Qualitative interpretation.

The highest-ranked positive chunk (chunk 4) occurs at the transition where the model reframes the equality

(z−r)​(z−s)​(z−t)=(z−c​r)​(z−c​s)​(z−c​t)(z-r)(z-s)(z-t)=(z-cr)(z-cs)(z-ct)

as a structural constraint on roots. For two monic cubic polynomials to be identical for all zz, their root multisets must coincide. Thus {r,s,t}\{r,s,t\} must equal {c​r,c​s,c​t}\{cr,cs,ct\} as a set. High positive DRTC on this structural equivalence step is consistent with it functioning as the key reasoning move in the rollout.

B.2 Ministral-3-3B

B.2.1 math_rollout_3295 (Ministral-3-3B)

Problem.

If f⁡(x)=1+x1−3​x,f1​(x)=f⁡(f⁡(x)),f2​(x)=f⁡(f1​(x)),f(x)=\frac{1+x}{1-3x},\ f_{1}(x)=f(f(x)),\ f_{2}(x)=f(f_{1}(x)), and in general fn​(x)=f⁡(fn−1​(x)),f_{n}(x)=f(f_{n-1}(x)), then f1993​(3)=f_{1993}(3)=

Gold answer.

15\frac{1}{5}

Opposing-sign chunks (directional tension).

This rollout is dominated by negative DRTC among the top-ranked chunks (e.g., chunks 9, 0, 10, 2, 37), meaning that masking these segments makes the pivot-local change more aligned with the realized rollout direction gg (after pivot weighting and relevance gating). The few positive chunks (notably chunks 6 and 5) indicate segments whose information flow steers pivot distributions along the realized direction, and thus act as the main “supporting” influences under DRTC.

Curvature diagnostic (geometry, not attribution).

CurvImpact reflects intervention-induced turning-angle changes in raw logit space. Here, several chunks with large |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}| (e.g., chunk 10 and chunk 7) coincide with moments where the trace shifts from informal planning toward explicit functional iteration/algebra, consistent with curvature capturing local reorientation intensity rather than directional sign. As elsewhere, CurvImpact is diagnostic and does not determine causal importance or steering direction.

Qualitative interpretation.

The most negative chunk (chunk 9: “maybe x=3x=3, but maybe it’s better …”) appears to reflect approach uncertainty and replanning; under DRTC, such segments counter-steer relative to the final realized solution direction. In contrast, the positive chunks (chunks 6 and 5) correspond to concretely computing early iterates and looking for a pattern, which matches the structure of the correct solution for this problem (a short periodic cycle under iteration). Overall, the sign pattern is consistent with a trace that contains nontrivial planning/hesitation, with the eventual correct branch supported by a smaller number of pattern-extraction steps.

B.2.2 math_rollout_3374 (Ministral-3-3B)

Problem.

When the base-16 number 666661666666_{16} is written in base 2, how many base-2 digits (bits) does it have?

Gold answer.

1919

Opposing-sign chunks (directional tension).

Most top-ranked chunks have positive DRTC (e.g., chunks 0, 6, 5, 8, 3, 13, 24, 30, 25), indicating that—after pivot weighting and relevance gating—their information flow tends to redirect pivot-local distributions in the same direction as the realized rollout. The highest-magnitude negative chunk (chunk 4) suggests a local segment whose contribution, when present, mildly steers opposite to the realized direction gg; here this is plausibly generic conversion boilerplate rather than a problem-specific constraint.

Curvature diagnostic (geometry, not attribution).

CurvImpact reflects turning-angle changes in raw logit space under the same pivot-local masking interventions. Several early chunks (e.g., chunk 0 and chunk 3) show relatively larger |CurvImpact||\mathrm{CurvImpact}|, consistent with curvature capturing local reorientation as the trace shifts from problem restatement to the base-conversion strategy. As elsewhere, curvature is diagnostic and does not determine causal sign.

Qualitative interpretation.

The dominant positive chunks center on the key structural fact 16=2416=2^{4} (chunk 5), which yields the baseline rule “each hex digit corresponds to 4 bits” and drives the initial estimate of 5×4=205\times 4=20 bits (chunks 24–25). The decisive correction is that the leading hex digit is 66 (binary 01100110), which does not contribute a leading 11 in the most significant position; thus the binary representation does not require the full 4 bits for the first digit. The high positive DRTC mass on these conversion-rule and correction steps is consistent with them forming the core solution logic in the realized rollout.

B.3 Phi-4-Mini

B.3.1 math_rollout_2757 (Phi-4-Mini)

Problem.

Let cc be a complex number. Suppose there exist distinct complex numbers rr, ss, and tt such that for every complex number zz, we have

(z−r)​(z−s)​(z−t)=(z−c​r)​(z−c​s)​(z−c​t).(z-r)(z-s)(z-t)=(z-cr)(z-cs)(z-ct).

Compute the number of distinct possible values of cc.

Gold answer.

44

Opposing-sign chunks (directional tension).

Most top-ranked chunks have negative DRTC (e.g., chunks 6, 10, 16, 19, 3, 17, 4, 2, 8), indicating that—after pivot weighting and relevance gating—their information flow tends to redirect pivot-local distributions opposite to the realized rollout direction gg. The main positive contributor (chunk 5) suggests a segment whose information flow supports the realized directional progression at the pivots that matter. As in all case studies, this sign pattern is about directional steering relative to the realized rollout, not an outcome-level correctness claim.

B.5 Qualitative evidence summary

Across all four models, the case studies suggest that high-magnitude DRTC chunks are not arbitrary: they frequently correspond to problem-specific constraints, reframing moves that set the intended strategy, or local correction steps that stabilize the subsequent derivation. When negative-sign chunks appear among the top contributors, their excerpts typically reflect competing framings, meta-level planning, or other detours whose presence (in the realized rollout) steers pivot-local distributions away from the realized direction. CurvImpact provides a complementary diagnostic view: large-magnitude CurvImpact often coincides with moments of local reorientation (e.g., restatement→\rightarrowstrategy, correction, or reinterpretation), but it is not used as an importance score. Overall, these qualitative patterns complement the quantitative results by supporting semantic plausibility while remaining agnostic to outcome-level causality and circuit identification.

Appendix C Expanded related work

Table 17 situates DRTC relative to recent frameworks for interpreting multi-step reasoning traces. We group prior work by its primary explanatory target and intervention style, and highlight what is unique about DRTC: (i) explicit pivot discovery to localize decision points, (ii) receiver-side interventions applied only at pivots that hold the realized prefix fixed and avoid generating a new continuation, (iii) signed directional steering in log-probability space, and (iv) curvature used strictly as an intervention-response diagnostic rather than an intrinsic importance score.

Appendix D Interactive inspection interface

Understanding long-horizon reasoning requires not only quantitative attribution scores but also tools for inspecting how those attributions relate to the model’s internal reasoning dynamics. To support qualitative verification of DRTC attributions and trajectory-level diagnostics, we provide an interactive inspection interface that links text spans, causal attribution scores, and geometric structure in the model’s reasoning trajectory.

We include representative static views of this interface here to illustrate how DRTC outputs can be examined by a human analyst. These figures are intended for qualitative inspection only and are not used to derive or validate any quantitative results in the paper. All quantitative results reported in the main text are computed directly from exported artifacts and CSV files, independent of the interface.

D.1 Textual reasoning with causal attribution

D.2 Trajectory geometry and attribution ranking

D.3 Interpretation and usage

Taken together, these views allow analysts to examine not only which reasoning steps causally influence a model’s trajectory, but also how those steps reshape the direction of reasoning over time. The interface supports bidirectional linking between text spans and trajectory geometry, enabling qualitative inspection of attribution results without relying solely on scalar importance measures.
